sections.h2: Does Massachusetts tax the gain when I sell a house?
sections.html:
Yes. The gain counts as income, though a seller of a main home can often keep much of it out of the calculation. The profit goes on your state return, and the Department of Revenue sets the rate by how long you held the property.

The same return reports everything else you earned that year, so a large sale can sit next to other income near the surtax threshold. Ask a preparer about timing before you sign.

Type of gainMassachusetts rate
Long-term capital gain5.00%
Short-term capital gain8.5%
Long-term gain on collectibles12.00%, with a 50% deduction
Extra surtax, tax year 20264% on income over $1,107,750

A house is not a collectible, so the 12 percent line matters only for items sold alongside a property.

Massachusetts follows the federal rule that lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of a principal residence, or $500,000 if you file jointly. The state conforms to Internal Revenue Code section 121 and applies it through M.G.L. c. 62, sections 1(c), 1(d) and 2(a).

  • It applies to a principal residence, so an investment property or a second home doesn't qualify.
  • The dollar caps are $250,000 for one filer and $500,000 for joint filers.
  • Any gain above the cap is taxed at the rate that fits the holding period.

Have a tax professional check the federal ownership and use tests before you count on the exclusion. Gather the closing statement, your purchase records and receipts for major improvements so the preparer can work out your gain.

A short checklist helps at the preparer's desk. Bring the settlement statement from the day you bought, the one from the sale, and records of the years you lived in the house as your main home. Add receipts for new roofs, additions or a new kitchen, since those raise your cost basis and shrink the gain. If you owned the house with someone else, each owner's share of the gain is figured on that owner's own return.

Selling a rental means no principal residence exclusion, so the entire gain faces the 5 percent or 8.5 percent rate. If you're selling a tenant-occupied house, the rate depends on your holding period.

Investors who hold a house for more than one year get the lower long-term rate, while gains on assets held a year or less fall in the 8.5 percent group. If your sale is near the one-year mark, check the exact dates with a tax adviser, because the rate difference is 3.5 percentage points on every taxable dollar.

Selling costs such as agent commissions and legal fees reduce the gain, so keep every closing document. If the house was a rental, ask the preparer how earlier depreciation affects the number, because that is a federal question that flows onto the state return. Planning the closing for a different calendar year can also move the gain into a lower-income year, which matters if you sit close to the surtax threshold.

The tax is due with your annual return, and April 15 is the deadline for the prior year. If you sell in the middle of a year and owe a large amount, estimated payments also come into play.

Estimated installments on Form 1-ES fall in these months:

  • April 15
  • June
  • September
  • January of the following year

An extension buys time to file but not time to pay, and interest runs on whatever is unpaid. It only counts if 80 percent of the liability is paid by the original date, and a payment of $5,000 or more with an extension has to go in electronically. Filing an extension with the IRS doesn't count as a Massachusetts extension. For payment questions, phone the Department of Revenue at (617) 887-6367, or toll free at (800) 392-6089 inside Massachusetts, weekdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

If a large gain lands in the middle of the year, work out the estimated payment right after the closing instead of waiting for the next return. Setting money aside from the proceeds at the closing table is simpler than finding it in April.

sections.h2: Deeds excise is a different tax
sections.html:
The deeds excise is a transfer tax on the sales price, and the capital gains tax is an income tax on your profit. The deeds excise is $2.28 per $500 of the sales price, less any mortgage assumed.

Even if your capital gain is fully excluded, the excise on the deed is a separate line at closing. Ask your closing attorney what applies to your deed. TIR 19-14 covers surcharge information.

sections.h2: Other steps that affect your net
sections.html:
Several state rules shape the timeline and your costs regardless of the tax result. Lawyers take part in nearly every Massachusetts sale, by law and by long habit. Deeds to 80 to 90 percent of properties are filed as recorded land at a county Registry of Deeds, while the rest is registered land documented by a Land Court certificate. The Secretary of the Commonwealth runs a service that emails you when a new document is recorded against your property, and deeds can be searched at masslandrecords.com.

Every sale also needs a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate of compliance from the local fire department, which charges a fee. Book that inspection the moment a closing date is set. Battery-powered smoke alarms that are more than ten years old or expired must be replaced with 10-year sealed, photoelectric units that have a hush feature.

Property tax is a separate matter from income tax. Boston's residential rate is $12.40 per $1,000, and Cambridge's FY2027 residential rate is $6.95 per $1,000. Those bills are separate from the gain.

An inherited house may carry a different set of questions, and the Massachusetts estate lien and release rules can also affect the closing. See our Massachusetts estate tax page for the $2,000,000 threshold, the $99,600 credit and the release of lien process, and our probate page for the court side.

Ask a Massachusetts tax preparer how the inherited basis works for your return. If the house needs work and you'd rather skip repairs, a cash sale as-is lets you close without fixing anything, though the smoke and carbon monoxide certificate still applies to the sale.

faqs.q: What is the Massachusetts capital gains tax rate on a house?
faqs.a: Long-term gains are taxed at 5.00 percent and short-term gains at 8.5 percent. A 4 percent surtax applies to income over $1,107,750 in tax year 2026.

faqs.q: How much gain can I exclude when I sell my main home in Massachusetts?
faqs.a: Up to $250,000, or $500,000 if you file jointly. Massachusetts conforms to Internal Revenue Code section 121 for this exclusion.

faqs.q: Is there a difference between short-term and long-term gains on a house?
faqs.a: Yes. Gains on assets held one year or less are taxed at 8.5 percent, while long-term gains are taxed at 5.00 percent. The difference is 3.5 percentage points on the taxable amount.

faqs.q: Do I owe the deeds excise even if my gain is excluded?
faqs.a: Yes, the deeds excise is a separate transfer tax. It is $2.28 per $500 of the sales price, less any mortgage assumed. Ask your closing attorney for the figure on your sale.

faqs.q: When do I pay Massachusetts tax on the gain?
faqs.a: With your annual return, due April 15 of the following year. For large gains, estimated payments on Form 1-ES may apply, and an extension to file doesn't extend the time to pay.
